prompt: Which statement gives the definition of agriculture used in this course?

options.text: The exclusive rearing of livestock for export earnings.
The science, art, and practice of cultivating plants and raising animals for food, fibre, medicine and other products used to sustain and enhance human life.
The commercial sale of processed foods in urban markets.
The laboratory study of soil chemistry and nothing beyond it.

explanation: Three words carry the definition: science, art and practice. It covers both plants and animals, and the purposes run wider than food alone, reaching fibre, medicine and other products that sustain and enhance human life.

why.a: Wrong. Livestock is only one half of the definition, and the word exclusive rules out crops entirely.
why.b: Correct. This is the definition word for word: science, art and practice, plants and animals, food, fibre, medicine and other products.
why.c: Wrong. Selling processed food is one activity inside the sector, not the definition of the sector.
why.d: Wrong. Soil chemistry belongs to soil management, which is one of the eleven aspects, not the whole field.

prompt: Agriculture is the science, art, and {{1}} of cultivating plants and raising animals.
explanation: Science, art and practice. Practice is the third word, and it is the one most often dropped when the definition is written from memory.

prompt: Agriculture is defined as the cultivation of plants only, and the raising of animals falls outside it.
explanation: The definition names both: cultivating plants and raising animals. Animal husbandry is also listed as one of the eleven key aspects.

why.true: Wrong. Nothing in the definition restricts agriculture to plants, and animal husbandry appears in the list of aspects.
why.false: Correct. The definition covers cultivating plants and raising animals together.

prompt: How does the course text describe the breadth of agriculture?

options.text: A narrow trade practised only by smallholders.
A single industry with one output, food.
A broad field that encompasses a wide range of activities, industries and sectors.
A branch of manufacturing with no biological component.

explanation: The opening sentence of the unit calls agriculture a broad field encompassing a wide range of activities, industries and sectors. That breadth is why the eleven aspects follow it.

why.a: Wrong. Narrow is the opposite of the word the text uses, which is broad.
why.b: Wrong. Food is one output among fibre, medicine and other products.
why.c: Correct. Broad field, wide range of activities, industries and sectors.
why.d: Wrong. The common factor across all agriculture is that it involves living organisms.

prompt: The course text lists {{1}} key aspects of agriculture.
explanation: Eleven, running from crop production to pest and disease management. Counting the list is the fastest way to check you have not dropped one when reciting it.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the key aspects of agriculture listed in the course text?

options.text: Agroforestry
Petroleum refining
Plant Breeding
Soil Management

explanation: The eleven aspects are crop production, animal husbandry, soil management, irrigation and water management, agricultural engineering, agroforestry, agricultural economics, food science and technology, sustainable and organic farming, plant breeding, and pest and disease management. Petroleum refining is not among them.

why.a: Wrong as an answer. Agroforestry, combining trees and crops for sustainable farming, is aspect six.
why.b: Correct. Petroleum refining belongs to no part of the list; it is the intruder.
why.c: Wrong as an answer. Plant breeding, developing new crop varieties, is aspect ten.
why.d: Wrong as an answer. Soil management, maintaining fertility and preventing erosion, is aspect three.

prompt: Match each aspect of agriculture to what the course text says it covers.

pairs.right: Growing cereals, fruits, vegetables and cash crops
Rearing livestock like cattle, poultry, sheep and fish
Maintaining soil fertility and preventing erosion
Development of farming tools, machinery and infrastructure

extraLabels: Combining trees and crops for sustainable farming
Processing, preserving and improving food products
explanation: Four of the eleven aspects with their own glosses. The two spare labels belong to agroforestry and to food science and technology.

prompt: Under which aspect of agriculture does growing cereals, fruits, vegetables and cash crops fall?

options.text: Crop Production
Agricultural Economics
Food Science and Technology
Agroforestry

explanation: Crop production is defined by exactly this list: cereals, fruits, vegetables and cash crops.

why.a: Correct. Cereals, fruits, vegetables and cash crops is the gloss on crop production.
why.b: Wrong. Agricultural economics is the business side, trade and markets.
why.c: Wrong. Food science and technology begins after harvest, with processing and preserving.
why.d: Wrong. Agroforestry is trees combined with crops, not crops on their own.

prompt: Animal {{1}} is the aspect of agriculture that rears livestock like cattle, poultry, sheep and fish.
explanation: Animal husbandry. Note that fish is listed inside it, which is why fish farming sits under agriculture at all.

prompt: Maintaining soil fertility and preventing erosion is the work of which aspect?

options.text: Irrigation and Water Management
Soil Management
Sustainable and Organic Farming
Pest and Disease Management

explanation: Soil management is given two jobs in the text: maintaining fertility and preventing erosion.

why.a: Wrong. Irrigation and water management is the efficient use of water for farming.
why.b: Correct. Fertility and erosion are the two words attached to soil management.
why.c: Wrong. Sustainable and organic farming is eco-friendly practice to protect the environment.
why.d: Wrong. Pest and disease management controls pests, diseases and weeds.

prompt: Which phrase does the course text attach to irrigation and water management?

options.text: Efficient use of water for farming
Complete removal of all water from the soil
Sale of water to urban households
Development of farming tools and machinery

explanation: Efficient use of water for farming. The word efficient is doing the work: the aspect is about using water well, not simply having it.

why.a: Correct. This is the gloss word for word.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Drainage of every drop would kill the crop.
why.c: Wrong. Selling water to households is not a farming activity at all.
why.d: Wrong. Tools and machinery belong to agricultural engineering.

prompt: Agricultural {{1}} covers the development of farming tools, machinery and infrastructure.
explanation: Agricultural engineering. Tools, machinery and infrastructure are its three words.

prompt: A farmer plants timber trees in rows between her cassava ridges so that both grow on the same land. Which aspect of agriculture is she practising?

options.text: Agroforestry, combining trees and crops for sustainable farming
Agricultural economics, the business aspects of farming
Plant breeding, developing new crop varieties
Soil management, maintaining fertility and preventing erosion

explanation: Trees and crops on the same land is agroforestry, defined in the text as combining trees and crops for sustainable farming.

why.a: Correct. Trees plus crops on one piece of land is the definition of agroforestry.
why.b: Wrong. Nothing in the scenario concerns trade, markets or the business of the farm.
why.c: Wrong. She is planting existing species, not developing a new variety.
why.d: Wrong. Soil may benefit, but the practice being named is the tree and crop combination itself.

prompt: Which aspect of agriculture covers the business aspects of farming, including trade and markets?

options.text: Agricultural Economics
Agricultural Engineering
Crop Production
Sustainable and Organic Farming

explanation: Agricultural economics. Trade and markets are named inside its gloss.

why.a: Correct. Business aspects of farming, including trade and markets.
why.b: Wrong. Engineering is tools, machinery and infrastructure.
why.c: Wrong. Crop production is growing the crops, not trading them.
why.d: Wrong. Sustainable and organic farming is about eco-friendly practice.

prompt: Processing, preserving and improving food products is the work of which aspect?

options.text: Food Science and Technology
Animal Husbandry
Irrigation and Water Management
Pest and Disease Management

explanation: Food science and technology carries three verbs in the text: processing, preserving and improving food products.

why.a: Correct. Processing, preserving and improving is its gloss word for word.
why.b: Wrong. Animal husbandry rears the livestock; it stops at the farm gate.
why.c: Wrong. Irrigation concerns water use, not food after harvest.
why.d: Wrong. Pest and disease management protects the crop and livestock, not the processed product.

prompt: Sustainable and organic farming is described as eco-friendly practices to protect the {{1}}.
explanation: The environment. Eco-friendly practices to protect the environment is the whole gloss.

prompt: Which specific branch of agriculture is responsible for developing new crop varieties to increase yield, enhance pest resistance, or improve environmental tolerance?

options.text: Plant Breeding
Soil Management
Agricultural Engineering
Agroforestry

explanation: Test 1, question 18, quoted as printed. The stem repeats the text word for word: plant breeding develops new crop varieties to increase yield, resistance to pests, or environmental tolerance.

why.a: Correct. New crop varieties, yield, pest resistance and environmental tolerance are all inside the definition of plant breeding.
why.b: Wrong. Soil management maintains fertility and prevents erosion; it does not create varieties.
why.c: Wrong. Agricultural engineering builds tools, machinery and infrastructure.
why.d: Wrong. Agroforestry combines trees and crops; it breeds nothing.

prompt: Developing new crop varieties to increase yield, resistance to pests, or environmental tolerance is the aspect called plant {{1}}.
explanation: Plant breeding. Three purposes travel with it: yield, pest resistance and environmental tolerance.

prompt: Pest and disease management is described as research into controlling which three things?

options.text: Pests, diseases and weeds in crops and livestock
Prices, demand and supply in rural markets
Soil, water and air on the farm
Tools, machinery and infrastructure

explanation: Pests, diseases and weeds, and in both crops and livestock. Weeds are the item most often forgotten.

why.a: Correct. The gloss names pests, diseases and weeds, in crops and livestock.
why.b: Wrong. Prices, demand and supply belong to agricultural economics.
why.c: Wrong. Soil and water each have their own aspect.
why.d: Wrong. Tools, machinery and infrastructure are agricultural engineering.

prompt: The aspects of agriculture are interconnected, and each contributes to the overall efficiency, sustainability and success of agriculture worldwide.
explanation: This is the closing sentence of the list, and it is the reason the unit goes on to show how livestock, crops and soil feed into one another.

why.true: Correct. The text says the areas are interconnected and each contributes to efficiency, sustainability and success worldwide.
why.false: Wrong. Nothing in the text treats the aspects as separate or independent; the opposite is stated.

prompt: Why is agriculture important, according to the in-text answer?

options.text: It plays a crucial role in feeding the global population, supporting economies, and ensuring food security.
It is the only sector that employs machinery.
It removes the need for any form of trade between nations.
It guarantees that no crop will ever fail.

explanation: Three things in one sentence: feeding the global population, supporting economies, and ensuring food security.

why.a: Correct. This is the in-text answer word for word.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Machinery is used across many sectors.
why.c: Wrong. Agriculture depends on trade rather than abolishing it.
why.d: Wrong, and an absolute. Risk management exists precisely because crops do fail.

prompt: Agriculture feeds the global population, supports economies and ensures food {{1}}.
explanation: Food security. It is the phrase the examiner reaches for again in Test 2, where food security is named as a major benefit of agripreneurship.

prompt: How does the course text link livestock farming to crop farming?

options.text: Livestock provide manure which enriches soil fertility, and crops can serve as fodder for animals.
Livestock and crops compete so directly that no farm should attempt both.
Crops must always be grown before any animal is introduced to a farm.
Livestock replace the need for soil fertility management entirely.

explanation: The link runs both ways: manure from the animals enriches the soil, and crop material feeds the animals. Integrated farming systems then optimise both.

why.a: Correct. Manure enriches fertility, crops serve as fodder, and integrated systems optimise both.
why.b: Wrong. The text presents them as complementary, not competing.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. No such ordering rule appears anywhere.
why.d: Wrong, and an absolute. Manure supports soil fertility; it does not remove the need to manage it.

prompt: Crops can serve as fodder for animals, and livestock in turn provide manure which enriches soil fertility.
explanation: Both halves are stated in the text, and together they are the standard illustration of how the aspects of agriculture interconnect.

why.true: Correct. Crops as fodder and manure enriching fertility are both given in the in-text answer.
why.false: Wrong. Denying either half contradicts the text directly.

prompt: Integrated farming systems {{1}} both crop and animal production.
explanation: Optimise. The point of integration is that neither side is run at the expense of the other.

prompt: What does the course text say determines crop yield?

options.text: Soil fertility
The number of workers on the farm
The distance to the nearest market
The brand of machinery used

explanation: Soil fertility determines crop yield. That single line is why soil management sits so early in the list of aspects.

why.a: Correct. The text states plainly that soil fertility determines crop yield.
why.b: Wrong. Labour matters to operations, but it is not what the text names here.
why.c: Wrong. Distance to market affects sales, not the yield in the field.
why.d: Wrong. Machinery belongs to agricultural engineering and is not named as the determinant of yield.

prompt: Which three practices does the course text name as improving soil quality?

options.text: Crop rotation, cover cropping and organic matter
Deep ploughing, burning and continuous monocropping
Heavy fertiliser use, irrigation and pesticide spraying
Fencing, drainage and mechanised harvesting

explanation: Crop rotation, cover cropping and organic matter. The text pairs them with a warning: overuse of fertilisers can degrade soil and affect long-term productivity.

why.a: Correct. These are the three practices named for improving soil quality.
why.b: Wrong. Continuous monocropping is the opposite of rotation.
why.c: Wrong. The text warns that overusing fertilisers degrades soil rather than improving it.
why.d: Wrong. These are farm operations, not the soil quality practices listed.

prompt: Overuse of fertilisers can degrade soil and affect long-term productivity.
explanation: The text says so directly, and it is the counterweight to the idea that more input always means more output.

why.true: Correct. Overuse of fertilisers degrades soil and affects long-term productivity.
why.false: Wrong. The text warns about fertiliser overuse in exactly these words.

prompt: A {{1}} is a person who engages in agriculture, raising living organisms for food or raw materials.
explanation: Farmer. Keep it apart from agripreneur, who is defined by identifying opportunities and applying entrepreneurial skills.

prompt: The glossary defines sustainability as managing resources like soil, water and biodiversity in ways that are:

options.text: Environmentally responsible, economically viable and socially equitable
Cheapest in the short term regardless of consequence
Entirely free of any human intervention
Focused only on maximum yield per hectare

explanation: Three legs: environmentally responsible, economically viable, socially equitable. Drop any one of them and it is not sustainability as the glossary defines it.

why.a: Correct. The glossary gives all three conditions together.
why.b: Wrong. Short-term cheapness is what sustainability is set against.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. Sustainability is about managing resources, which is intervention.
why.d: Wrong. Yield alone ignores the environmental and social legs.

prompt: Modern agriculture consists of interconnected sectors rather than isolated industries. Which example best demonstrates this interconnectedness?

options.text: Livestock and crop farming are linked because crop residues can feed livestock, manure can support soil health, and healthy soils contribute to crop protection.
Residential architecture and cellular communication protocols.
Deep-sea petroleum drilling and international tourism visa regulations.
Mineral extraction and international currency trading.

explanation: Test 2, question 18, quoted as printed and confirmed correct on the graded paper. Only the crop residues and manure answer is about agriculture at all; the other three pair industries that have nothing to do with farming or with each other.

why.a: Correct. Crop residues feed livestock, manure supports soil health, healthy soils protect crops: the loop the text describes.
why.b: Wrong. Neither architecture nor communication protocols is an agricultural sector.
why.c: Wrong. Petroleum drilling and visa regulation are outside agriculture entirely.
why.d: Wrong. Mining and currency trading demonstrate nothing about agricultural interconnection.

prompt: Crop {{1}} can feed livestock, manure can support soil health, and healthy soils contribute to crop protection.
explanation: Residues. The examiner's own wording in Test 2 for what the text calls crops serving as fodder.

prompt: What does the unit give as the common factor for all operators in agriculture?

options.text: That rearing, cultivation, harvesting or cropping of plants and animals involves living organisms
That every operator must own land outright
That all agricultural output must be exported
That every farm must be mechanised

explanation: Living organisms. That is why timing matters: there is a seed time and a harvest time, and care must be taken in between.

why.a: Correct. The introduction names living organisms as the common factor for every operator.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Land tenure is listed elsewhere as a problem, not a defining requirement.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. Export is one market among local, wholesale and online.
why.d: Wrong, and an absolute. Mechanisation is a technology trend, not a defining factor.

prompt: Whatever form of agriculture you are in, there is a seed time and a {{1}} time, during which care must be taken to enhance optimal yield.
explanation: Harvest time. Seed time and harvest time bracket the period in which care determines the yield.

prompt: A research team develops a cassava variety that survives longer dry spells, while a second team designs a solar dryer for the harvested roots. Which two aspects of agriculture are these, in that order?

options.text: Plant Breeding, then Food Science and Technology
Agroforestry, then Agricultural Engineering
Soil Management, then Agricultural Economics
Pest and Disease Management, then Crop Production

explanation: Developing a variety with better environmental tolerance is plant breeding. Drying the harvested roots is processing and preserving, which is food science and technology.

why.a: Correct. A new variety with environmental tolerance is plant breeding; drying to preserve is food science and technology.
why.b: Wrong. No trees are combined with crops, and the dryer preserves food rather than being farm infrastructure.
why.c: Wrong. Neither team is working on fertility, erosion, trade or markets.
why.d: Wrong. Drought tolerance is not pest control, and drying is not crop production.

prompt: Agriculture is {{1}}, and it covers {{2}}.

accept: the science, art, and practice of cultivating plants and raising animals
choices: the science, art, and practice of cultivating plants and raising animals
the commercial distribution of food to urban consumers
the mechanised production of fibre for industry alone
the government regulation of rural land ownership

accept: food, fibre, medicine and other products used to sustain and enhance human life
choices: food, fibre, medicine and other products used to sustain and enhance human life
food and nothing else, since fibre and medicine are industrial concerns
export commodities only, because local sales are not agriculture
livestock products only, because crops belong to horticulture

explanation: The definition in two halves: what agriculture is, and what it is for. Both halves are examinable, and the second is the one candidates shorten to food.

prompt: Which pair of aspects sits closest to the farm gate on the output side, that is, after the crop has been grown?

options.text: Food Science and Technology, and Agricultural Economics
Soil Management, and Irrigation and Water Management
Crop Production, and Animal Husbandry
Plant Breeding, and Agroforestry

explanation: Food science and technology processes and preserves what has been grown, and agricultural economics trades it. The other three pairs all sit before or during production.

why.a: Correct. Processing and preserving, then trade and markets, both come after the crop exists.
why.b: Wrong. Soil and water are managed to produce the crop in the first place.
why.c: Wrong. These are production itself, not what follows it.
why.d: Wrong. Breeding precedes planting, and agroforestry is a way of growing.

prompt: Fish is named inside the gloss on animal husbandry, alongside cattle, poultry and sheep.
explanation: Rearing livestock like cattle, poultry, sheep and fish. That single word is the bridge from Module One to the whole of Module Two.

why.true: Correct. The gloss on animal husbandry names cattle, poultry, sheep and fish.
why.false: Wrong. Fish appears in that list, which is why fish farming is treated as a branch of agriculture.

prompt: Pest and disease management is research into controlling pests, diseases and {{1}} in crops and livestock.
explanation: Weeds. The aspect is named for pests and diseases, but weeds are inside its definition and are the item most often left out.

prompt: A distractor in this course often looks right because it is absolute. Which of these importance statements is the one the text actually makes?

options.text: Agriculture alone guarantees that no nation will ever import food.
Agriculture plays a crucial role in feeding the global population, supporting economies, and ensuring food security.
Agriculture entirely removes the need for economic policy in rural areas.
Agriculture is important solely because of its contribution to export earnings.

explanation: The measured, three-part statement is the one in the text. The others each hang on an absolute: alone, entirely, solely. That pattern repeats through both computer-based tests.

why.a: Wrong. Alone and never are absolutes, and Nigeria's own fish deficit shows imports continue.
why.b: Correct. Feeding the global population, supporting economies, ensuring food security.
why.c: Wrong. Entirely is an absolute, and policy and advocacy is itself a value chain segment.
why.d: Wrong. Solely is an absolute, and export is one market among local, wholesale and online.
